audit.recode_to: Contemporary Enggano (the living language under engg1245): fixed final stress, final stress, secondary stress alternating right-to-left, per Yoder 2011:37 (instrumental). If the record is meant to describe Kähler's 1930s 'Old Enggano' doculect instead, keep penultimate but drop 'strict' (Kähler: 'generally'; suffixed forms 'sometimes' keep original stress; enclitics =dia/=dai/=du leave stress pre-penultimate, e.g. eúbadia — Kähler 1940:96 via Hemmings & Arka 2023) and add a caution that the modern language has final stress. Either way add Yoder 2011 as a contra/caution.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on p. 6 of the held Burleigh & Dalrymple translation of Kähler 1940, as cited. (2) The deciding source is a 1940 grammar sketch of 1937-38 Enggano whose stress statement is hedged ('generally', 'often.. but sometimes'), yet the catalog codes 'fixed-strict' penultimate. (3) The best available stress description, Yoder 2011 (Glottolog's first-ranked phonology ref, 147 pp, acoustic measurements, downloaded now), states that stress in Enggano as spoken today is consistently word-final in mono- and polymorphemic words and in loans, and explicitly notes the change from Kähler's penultimate pattern; the 1895 Holle list already reported penultimate-or-final. Hemmings & Arka 2023 (downloaded) confirm for Old Enggano that certain enclitics did not shift stress, so even the 1940 doculect was not 'strict'. (4) Hence at-risk: a better, held-as-of-now so

In Enggano this generally lies on the vowel of the penultimate syllable. If a word is extended by suffixes, the accent is often placed on the vowel of the penultimate syllable, but sometimes remains on the original syllable.' Identical in lines 250-254. sources.quote: For Old Enggano (restating Kähler 1940:96): 'In most cases, the process of suffixation triggers stress shift, so that the stress is on the penultimate syllable. However, the enclitics =dia, =dai and =du do not trigger this same process, with stress remaining on the [u] vowel' (eúbadia, eúbadai, eúbadu). No statement on contemporary stress position; notes vowel reduction 'in non-stressed syllables' and regular final-vowel loss in Contemporary Enggano.
